title: The Story of Sir Pellias: Chapter 5
paragraphs: _How Sir Gawaine met Sir Pellias, and how he promised to help him with the Lady Ettard._

After the wonderful lady had vanished from their sight, the three knights stood for a little while completely astonished. They could hardly believe what their eyes had seen. Then Sir Gawaine spoke. “Truly, that was a strange thing that happened to us. In all my life I have never known such a marvel. It is plain that some fine adventure lies in what we have seen. So let us ride down into that valley, where we will surely find out what it all means. I swear I have hardly ever seen a knight as fearsomely strong as the one who just fought that battle. So I cannot understand why he gave himself up to his enemies, when he had almost won the victory over them.”
Sir Ewaine and Sir Marhaus agreed that it would be good to go down and ask what the sight they had witnessed could mean.
So the three of them and their attendants rode down into the valley.
They rode on until they came to a clearing among the trees. There they saw three fine tents standing together. One was made of white cloth, the second of green cloth, and the third of scarlet cloth.

As the three companions came near the tents, two knights came out to meet them. Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine saw the shields of the two and knew at once that they were Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte. Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte knew Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine just as quickly. Each side was greatly surprised to meet the other in so strange a place. When they came together they greeted one another joyfully and clasped hands with warm love and good fellowship.

Then Sir Gawaine introduced Sir Marhaus to Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte. The five knights went together into the tents, talking happily and pleasantly as they walked. In the tent of Sir Brandiles they found a good meal laid out, with white bread and wine of excellent flavor.

After a while Sir Gawaine said to Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte, “Sirs, a little while ago we saw a very strange thing. We stood together on top of that hill and looked down into this plain. There we saw a single knight dressed all in red armor, fighting ten knights. That one knight in red fought the ten so fiercely that he drove them all away from him, though they were so many and he was alone. I swear I have hardly ever seen a knight show such great skill in arms. Yet when he had beaten all but two of those knights, and was well on his way to a clear victory, he suddenly gave himself up to those two. He let them take him, bind him, and drive him shamefully from the field. Now, I beg you, tell me what it meant. Who was that knight who fought so great a battle and then surrendered so shamefully?”

At this Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte gave no answer. They looked the other way, for they did not know what to say. When Sir Gawaine saw that they were embarrassed, he began to wonder more than ever what the matter meant, and he said, “What is this? Why do you not answer me? I order you to tell me what your looks mean, and who that red knight is!”
After a while Sir Mador de la Porte said, “I will not tell you, but you may come and see.”

Then Sir Gawaine began to think that there might be something here that was better not made public. Perhaps, he thought, he had best look into the matter alone. So he said to the other knights, “Wait here a little, Sirs, and I will go with Sir Mador de la Porte.”
So Sir Gawaine went with Sir Mador de la Porte, and Sir Mador led him to the white tent. When they got there, Sir Mador drew aside the curtains of the tent. “Go in!” he said, and Sir Gawaine went in.

Inside the tent he saw a man sitting on a couch of rushes covered with blue cloth. Soon he saw that the man was Sir Pellias. But Sir Pellias did not see him at first. He sat with his head bowed, like a man completely crushed by despair.
When Sir Gawaine saw who it was sitting on the couch, he was greatly amazed and cried out, “Ha! Is it you, Sir Pellias? Is it you?”

But when Sir Pellias heard Sir Gawaine’s voice and saw who had spoken to him, he gave a very bitter cry. He sprang to his feet and ran as far away as the walls of the tent would allow. Then he turned his face to the wall.

After a while Sir Gawaine spoke very sternly to Sir Pellias. “Sir, I am astonished and deeply ashamed that a Knight of King Arthur’s Royal Court and of his Round Table should behave so dishonorably, as I saw you behave today. It is hard to believe that a knight of such fame and nobility as you would let two unknown knights take and bind him, as you did today. How could you bring yourself to accept such insult and shame? Now I demand that you explain this matter to me.”
But Sir Pellias was silent and would not reply. Then Sir Gawaine cried out fiercely, “Ha! Will you not answer me?” And Sir Pellias shook his head.

Then Sir Gawaine spoke again, still very fiercely. “Sir! You will answer me one way or another! Either you will tell me the meaning of your shameful conduct, or you will fight me to the death. I will not let you bring such shame on King Arthur and his Round Table without defending their honor and good name myself. Once you and I were dear friends. But unless you clear yourself at once, I will despise you and count you as my enemy.”

At this Sir Pellias spoke like a man nearly out of his mind. “I will tell you everything,” he said. Then he confessed it all to Sir Gawaine. He told everything that had happened to him since he left the May Court of Queen Guinevere to begin this adventure, and Sir Gawaine listened in great amazement. When Sir Pellias had finished telling all that had befallen him, Sir Gawaine said, “Truly, this is very strange. I cannot understand how you came to be so caught up in the charms of this lady, unless she has bewitched you with some powerful enchantment.”
To this Sir Pellias said, “Yes, I believe I have been bewitched. I am completely beside myself in this matter, and I cannot control my passion.”

Then Sir Gawaine thought for a long while, considering the matter very seriously. By and by he said, “I have a plan, and it is this. I will go to the Lady Ettard myself and look carefully into this affair. If I find that anyone has tangled you in enchantments, I will make that person suffer greatly for it. I will not allow another enchanter to trick you, as one has already tricked Merlin the Wise.”
Then Sir Pellias said to Sir Gawaine, “How will you manage to come into the presence of the Lady Ettard?”

Sir Gawaine replied, “I will tell you. We two will trade armor, and I will go to the castle wearing yours. When I get there, I will say that I beat you in a fight and took your armor from you. Then they will perhaps let me into the castle to tell my story, and I will have a chance to speak with her.”
Then Sir Pellias said, “Very well. It shall be as you say.”

So Sir Pellias called an esquire, and Sir Gawaine called his own esquire. The two of them took the armor off Sir Pellias and dressed Sir Gawaine in it. After that, Sir Gawaine mounted the horse of Sir Pellias and rode openly into the field where Sir Pellias had paraded before.

Now, the Lady Ettard happened to be walking at that time on a platform inside the castle walls, from which she looked down into the meadow. When she saw a red knight parading in the meadow, she thought Sir Pellias had come back again. She was annoyed and insulted beyond all measure. So she said to those near her, “That knight upsets me so badly that I fear I will fall ill from it if he comes here many more times. I wish I knew how to be rid of him. Only an hour ago I sent ten good knights against him, and he beat them all very swiftly, to their great shame and to mine.”

So she beckoned to the Red Knight, and when he had come near the castle walls, she said to him, “Sir Knight, why do you keep coming here to trouble and insult me like this? Can you not understand that the more often you come to tease me in this way, the more I hate you?”

Then Sir Gawaine lifted the visor of his helmet and showed his face, and the Lady Ettard saw that the Red Knight was not Sir Pellias. Sir Gawaine said, “Lady, I am not the one you take me for, but another. Look! I wear your enemy’s armor on my body, so you can see that I have beaten him. You must think it hardly likely that I could wear his armor unless I won it from him by force of arms. So you need trouble yourself no more about him.”

Then the Lady Ettard could only believe that this knight, whom she did not know, had truly defeated Sir Pellias in a fight and taken his armor from him. She was very astonished that such a thing could have happened. To her, Sir Pellias had seemed one of the greatest knights in the world, so she wondered who this knight could be who had beaten him in battle. She ordered several of her attendants to go out and bring that red knight into the castle and to treat him with great honor. He must surely be one of the greatest champions in the world.

So Sir Gawaine came into the castle and was brought before the Lady Ettard, who stood in a very large and noble hall. The hall was lit by seven tall windows of colored glass, and it was hung all around with rich tapestries of excellent quality. Sir Gawaine was greatly amazed at the splendor of everything he saw there.

Sir Gawaine had taken the helmet off his head and carried it under his arm, against his hip. His head was bare, so that everyone there could see his face plainly. They all saw that he was very handsome, with eyes as blue as steel, a high, curved nose, and dark, rich hair and beard. His bearing was steady and proud, so that those who looked at him were awed by his knightly appearance.

Then the Lady Ettard came to Sir Gawaine and gave him her hand, and he knelt and kissed it. The lady spoke to him very graciously. “Sir Knight, it would give me great pleasure if you would tell us your name and declare your rank to us.”
To this Sir Gawaine replied, “Lady, I cannot tell you these things at present, for I am just now bound by a vow of secrecy on those points. So I beg you to be patient with me for a little while.”

Then the Lady Ettard said, “Sir Knight, it is a great pity that we may not know your name and rank. Even so, though we do not yet know who you are, I hope you will give us the pleasure of your company for a while. I hope you will be kind enough to stay in this humble place for two or three days, while we offer you such refreshment as we are able to give.”

Now a very unfortunate thing happened. The Lady Ettard had grown so fond of the necklace of emeralds, opal stones and gold that she had borrowed from Sir Pellias that she never let it leave her, by day or by night. So she was wearing it at that moment, hanging about her neck and throat. As she talked with Sir Gawaine, he looked at that necklace, and its enchantment began to take a strong hold on him. He began to feel as though his heart were being drawn out of his chest toward the Lady Ettard, so that before long he could not keep his eyes from her. The more he looked at the necklace and the lady, the more the enchantment of the jewel took hold of his spirit. So when the Lady Ettard spoke so kindly to him, he was very glad to accept her kindness. Gazing at her with great longing, he said, “Lady, you are very gentle to offer me such courtesy. I will be glad beyond measure to stay with you for a short while.”

At these words the Lady Ettard was very pleased. She said to herself, “Truly, this knight, though I do not know who he may be, must be a champion of extraordinary strength and great achievements. If I can persuade him to stay in this castle as my champion, I will surely gain great credit by it. I will have someone to defend my rights who must surely be the greatest knight in all the world.” So she showed every charm and grace of manner to please Sir Gawaine, and Sir Gawaine was completely delighted by her kindness.

Sir Engamore was there at that time, and he was deeply troubled. The more courtesy Sir Gawaine received from the Lady Ettard, the more Sir Engamore sank into sorrow and distress, so much so that it was pitiful to see. He said to himself, “Before these foreign knights came here, the Lady Ettard was very kind to me, and was willing to take me as her champion and lord. But first Sir Pellias came and beat me, and now this strange knight comes and beats him. In the presence of such a great champion as this, I have become nothing in her sight.” So Sir Engamore left that place and went to his private room, where he sat down alone in great sorrow.

The Lady Ettard had ordered a very noble and splendid feast to be prepared for Sir Gawaine and herself. While it was being made ready, she and Sir Gawaine walked together in the pleasure garden of the castle. It was a pleasant, shady place where flowers grew in great numbers, and many birds sang sweetly among the blossoms of the trees. As Sir Gawaine and the lady walked there together, the attendants stood a little way off and watched them. They said to one another, “It would surely be a very good thing if the Lady Ettard took this knight as her champion, and if he stayed here in Grantmesnle forever.”

Sir Gawaine and the lady walked together, talking cheerfully, until sunset. By then supper was ready, and they went in and sat down to eat. While they ate, a number of handsome pages played harps before them, and several damsels sang sweetly to the music. Sir Gawaine’s heart swelled with joy. He said to himself, “Why should I ever leave this place? Look, I have been banished from King Arthur’s Court. Why should I not set up a Court of my own here, one that might in time be as glorious as his?” The Lady Ettard looked so beautiful to him that this seemed a wonderfully pleasant idea.
Now let us turn to Sir Pellias.

After Sir Gawaine had left him, Sir Pellias began to fear that he had not been wise. At last he said to himself, “Suppose Sir Gawaine forgets his duty to me when he meets the Lady Ettard. It seems she may have some powerful charm that could draw Sir Gawaine’s heart to her. If he comes under the spell of such enchantment, he may forget his duty to me and betray the honor of his knighthood.”

The more Sir Pellias thought about this, the more troubled he became. So when evening had fallen, he called an esquire to him and said, “Go and bring me the clothing of a black friar, for I want to go to the castle of Grantmesnle in disguise.” The esquire did as he was told and brought him the clothing, and Sir Pellias dressed himself in it.

By that time darkness had covered the whole earth, so no one could have recognized Sir Pellias even if they had seen his face. He went to the castle, and the people there, who thought he was a black friar, as he looked to be, let him in by the small back gate.

As soon as Sir Pellias was inside the castle, he began to ask carefully where he could find the knight who had come there that afternoon. The people in the castle still thought he was a friar of the black order, and they said to him, “What do you want with that knight?” Sir Pellias answered, “I have a message for him.” They said, “You cannot see that knight just now. He is at supper with the Lady Ettard, and he is talking pleasantly with her.”

At this Sir Pellias grew very angry, for he hated the thought that Sir Gawaine was making merry with the Lady Ettard at that very moment. He said sternly, “I must speak with that knight right now, so I order you to take me to him without delay.” Then the people of the castle said, “Wait here, and we will see whether that knight is willing to have you come to him.”

One of the attendants went to the place where Sir Gawaine sat at supper with the Lady Ettard, and he said, “Sir Knight, a black friar has come here who demands to speak with you right away. He will not be refused, and he keeps repeating his demand.”

At this Sir Gawaine felt a great pang of conscience, for he knew he was not treating Sir Pellias honorably. He wondered whether this black friar might be a messenger from his friend. Yet he could not see how he could refuse to speak with such a messenger. So after thinking for a while, he said, “Bring the black friar here, and let him give me his message.”

So the attendants brought Sir Pellias, dressed as a black friar, to the outer room next to where Sir Gawaine sat at supper with the lady. For a little while Sir Pellias did not go in. He stood behind the curtain of the ante-room and watched them, because he wanted to be sure whether Sir Gawaine was true to him or not.

Everything in the room where the knight and the lady sat was decorated with extraordinary splendor. It was lit by several score of wax candles, which gave off a delightful perfume as they burned. As Sir Pellias stood behind the curtains, he saw Sir Gawaine and the Lady Ettard sitting at the table together, and he saw how happy they were in each other’s company. He saw that Sir Gawaine and the lady drank wine from the same cup, and that the cup was made of gold. As he watched the two of them making merry together, he was filled with great anger and outrage, for now he understood that Sir Gawaine had betrayed him.

After a while he could hold himself back no longer. He took five steps into the room and stood before Sir Gawaine and the Lady Ettard. They looked up at him in great surprise, and he threw back the hood from his face, and they knew him. The Lady Ettard shrieked loudly, crying out, “I have been betrayed!” Sir Gawaine sat completely silent, for he had not a single word to say to the lady or to Sir Pellias.

Then Sir Pellias went close to the Lady Ettard with such a fierce look on his face that she could not move for fear. When he stood next to her, he seized the necklace of emeralds, opal stones and gold so violently that the clasp broke and he pulled it from her neck. He said, “This is mine, and you have no right to it!” And with that he thrust it into his bosom. Then he turned on Sir Gawaine where he sat and said, “You are false both to your knighthood and to your friendship, for you have betrayed me completely.” Then he raised his arm and struck Sir Gawaine in the face with the back of his hand so hard that the mark of his fingers was left in red across Sir Gawaine’s cheek.

Sir Gawaine turned pale as ashes and cried out, “Sir, I have truly betrayed you, but you have insulted me so much that we are even.” Sir Pellias answered, “Not so. The injury I gave you is only on your cheek, but the injury you gave me is on my heart. Nevertheless, I will answer to you for the insult I have done you. But you must also answer to me for the wrong you have done me by betraying me.”

Then Sir Gawaine said, “I am willing to answer to you in full.” And Sir Pellias said, “You will indeed.” With that he turned and left the place, and he did not even look back at Sir Gawaine or at the Lady Ettard.

But now that the Lady Ettard no longer wore the magic collar around her neck, Sir Gawaine felt nothing of the great enchantment that had drawn him so strongly to her before. He now disliked her as much as he had liked her before. So he said to himself, “How could I have betrayed my knighthood for this lady, and done so much harm to my friend?” He pushed back his chair violently and rose from the table, meaning to leave her.

But when the Lady Ettard saw what he meant to do, she spoke to him in great anger. She was deeply insulted that he had deceived her when he said he had defeated Sir Pellias. She said hotly, “You may go, and I am quite willing for you to do so, for you lied when you told me you had defeated Sir Pellias. Now I see that he is both a stronger and a nobler knight than you. He struck you as if you were his servant, and you still wear the marks of his fingers on your cheek.”

At this Sir Gawaine was furiously angry and filled with shame at what had happened to him. He said, “Lady, I think you have bewitched me and brought me to this point of dishonor. As for Sir Pellias, look out into that meadow tomorrow and see whether I do not leave a deeper mark on him than he ever left on me.” Then he left the room, went down into the courtyard, and called to the attendants there to bring him his horse. They did as he ordered, and he rode out into the night at once.

He was very glad of the darkness of the night, for it seemed easier to bear his shame in the dark. When he came to the glade of trees, he would not enter the pavilion where his friends were. When Sir Ewaine and Sir Marhaus came out to him and told him to come in, he would not, but stayed outside in the darkness. He said to himself, “If I go in where there is light, perhaps they will see the mark of Sir Pellias’s hand on my face.”
So he stayed outside in the darkness and told them to go away and leave him alone.

Once they had gone, Sir Gawaine summoned his esquire and said, “Help me out of this red armor and carry it to the pavilion of Sir Pellias, because I hate the sight of it.” The esquire obeyed, and Sir Gawaine paced back and forth all night long, his mind and heart heavy with trouble.
